unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 5: Money Matters. Money is a part of everyday life, but understanding how it works is a skill that takes practice. Whether you are saving coins in a jar at home, choosing between two things you want at the market, or hearing adults talk about bills and budgets, money is always around you. In this unit, you will explore the world of financial literacy — the ability to understand and use money wisely.
unit.learningPath: Begin with the Vocabulary companion and learn the twenty-eight unit words a few at a time, saying each example aloud. Work through the Grammar companion, focusing on comparative adverbs, quantifiers and reflexive pronouns. Read "Money, Markets, and Making Good Choices" and the two-part story "The Notice Board", answering the comprehension questions with evidence from the text. Complete the grammar practice, the opinion-essay writing workshop and the speaking tasks, then finish with the quiz and the Check Your Learning self-assessment.

readings.title: Money, Markets, and Making Good Choices
readings.setting: A market town in East Africa
readings.passageScript:
Every morning in cities and towns across East Africa, markets come alive. Stalls are set up with colourful fabrics, fresh fruit, and bags of rice and sugar. Shopkeepers call out prices. Customers count their coins carefully. A woman buys enough flour for the week. A boy saves his last few shillings instead of buying sweets. A grandmother bargains firmly for a fair price on vegetables. Money moves from hand to hand, and each decision — big or small — tells a story about how people think about value.
But what is money, really? Money is a tool. It is not good or bad on its own. What matters is how we use it. Financial literacy means understanding how money works and learning to make smart choices with it. This includes knowing the difference between needs and wants. A need is something you must have to live safely and healthily, like food, clean water, shelter, and clothing. A want is something nice to have but not essential, like a new toy, a fancy phone case, or extra sweets after school.
One of the most crucial money skills is saving. Saving means putting aside part of your money for the future instead of spending it all at once. Even small amounts add up over time. If you save just a few coins each week, after several months you might have enough for something substantial — a book you have wanted, a gift for someone you love, or a contribution to a family goal. Many families teach children to be balanced with money: not to waste it, not to hoard it selfishly, and to share with those who have less. A wise saying reminds us that the best people are those who are most useful to others. Giving to charity is not only generous — it is a thoughtful way of using what we have and strengthening our community.
A budget is a plan for how to use your money. Even young people can make a simple budget. Imagine you receive some pocket money each week. You could divide it into three parts: one part for saving, one part for spending on things you need or enjoy, and one part for giving to charity or helping your family. This simple plan helps you feel in control and teaches you to think carefully about your resources. People who budget well are often more productive with their money than people who spend without thinking.
Another important skill is learning to compare prices. When you go to the market with your family, you might notice that one shop sells rice more cheaply than another, or that one brand of soap lasts longer than a cheaper one. Comparing carefully means you get better value. This is a form of critical thinking — the same skill you use in school when you adapt your ideas based on new information.
Money can sometimes cause stress, especially for families who do not have much. It is important to be sensitive to this. Not everyone has the same amount, and that is nothing to feel uncomfortable about. What matters is being humble, grateful for what you have, and wise with whatever resources are available to you. A person who manages a meagre income well can be far more successful than someone who wastes a large fortune.
Understanding money is a privilege and a responsibility. The earlier you start learning, the better prepared you will be. Whether you are saving for a family celebration, helping with the shopping, or simply choosing between two treats at the corner shop, every choice you make is practice for the bigger decisions ahead.

readings.title: A Conversation About Saving
readings.passageScript:
Maya and Sami are talking after class about pocket money and saving.
Maya: Sami, do you get pocket money from your parents?
Sami: Yes, I get a small amount each week. But I do not spend it all. I save most of it in a tin under my bed.
Maya: Really? I find it hard to save. I usually spend mine at the school tuck shop. Sometimes I buy snacks I do not even need!
Sami: I used to do that too. But my grandmother told me, 'Teach yourself to wait. If you still want it after three days, then buy it.' That advice changed how I think about money.
Maya: That is clever! So you save more patiently than before?
Sami: Yes, much more patiently. Before the New Year, I had saved enough to buy small gifts for both my parents. I felt really proud of myself.
Maya: That is lovely. I want to start saving more carefully too. Maybe I will make myself a budget, like the one we planned in class.
Sami: You should! Even a few coins a week add up. Neither of us is too young to learn about money.
Maya: Firstly, I will spend less at the tuck shop. In addition, I will save a little every week. Both plans will help me reach my goal more quickly than before.
Sami: That sounds sensible. If we save carefully now, we will make wiser choices when we are older.

readings.title: The Notice Board, part 1
readings.passageScript:
The first day at Mbali Academy was not what Amal expected.
She had been eagerly waiting to move into the school dormitory for weeks. Her mother said it would help her become more independent. Her father, who rarely shared his feelings, simply hugged her and said, "Remember who you are."
Amal was not sure what that meant. But she promised herself she would try.
Mbali Academy was a massive, stone-walled school perched on a green ridge. It was known for its fabulous science programme and its strict rules. Students wore uniforms and ate in long rows. The dormitories were clean but cold.
Her roommate was a girl named Nora, who talked firmly and fast.
"Don't touch my shelf," Nora said the moment Amal entered.
Amal smiled shyly. "I won't."
She unpacked her meagre belongings — two books, a tiny photo frame, and a borrowed jumper. Compared to Nora's colourful bedding and shiny decorations, Amal's side looked bare.
At dinner, Amal tried to talk to others. But most were already in their own friend groups. She felt a little uncomfortable, like a chair with one short leg.
"Just give it time," she told herself.
Later that week, a teacher announced that a new student council would be formed. "One student will be chosen from each dormitory group. They will help represent your voices and ideas."
Amal's ears perked up. Maybe this was her chance to be part of something.
The next morning, Amal saw a poster on the school notice board. "Nominate a student who shows leadership, kindness, and courage."
Nora and her friends giggled behind her.
"We already know who will win," Nora said. "Maya. Everyone likes her."
Amal looked at the names scribbled on the board. All were from the same friend group. None were new students. None were like her.
That night, she asked herself a question: should I try anyway?
"I don't belong," she whispered, frustrated.
But something inside her — small but substantial — told her to speak. She wrote her name in shaky handwriting.
The next day, whispers started. "Who is that girl?" someone asked.
"Amal," another replied. "Isn't she the one with the second-hand jumper?"
Nora rolled her eyes. "That's a questionable choice." Amal felt heat in her chest. She thought about removing her name. But a teacher passed by and said, "I saw your name. Good for you."
Amal smiled, just a little.
The council speeches were set for Friday. Students would gather in the hall. Each candidate had to give a short talk.
Amal felt as if her stomach had flipped. She barely slept on Thursday night.
"You don't have to do this," Nora said in the morning. "It's not too late to back out."
Amal looked at her reflection in the mirror. "I didn't come here to hide," she said quietly.

readings.title: The Notice Board, part 2
readings.passageScript:
She remembered what her father had said.
When it was her turn to speak, Amal walked slowly to the front. Her paper trembled in her hands. She breathed in.
"My name is Amal. I'm new here, and I know I don't have a big group of friends yet. But I believe kindness should be a rule, not a suggestion."
She paused.
"Sometimes rules feel unavoidable, but that doesn't make them right. Some are even unconstitutional — they go against fairness."
The room was silent.
"I've felt frustrated and small here. But I've also learned that even small voices can grow. I will do my best to be fair, hospitable, and honest."
She stepped back. Her knees felt wobbly. The applause was quiet — but real.
Later, someone tapped her shoulder. A younger girl from another dormitory. "Thank you," the girl said. "I felt sensitive when I arrived too. You made me feel seen."
Amal smiled wide. It was not a massive moment, but it felt crucial.
Voting happened the next day. When the results were posted, Amal was not the winner. Maya had the most votes. But below her name, another line had been added: "Amal: assistant representative for dormitory two."
Amal nodded. "Maybe the rules adapted."
In the weeks that followed, she helped organise weekend activities, sorted out complaints, and reminded teachers when supplies were unavailable. She took the job seriously and learned quickly.
She noticed that when she spoke firmly, people listened. When she spoke aggressively, they pushed back. When she spoke dramatically, they laughed. She started choosing her tone more carefully.
One day, a rule was posted on the notice board: "Only students with full uniforms may attend weekend outings."
Several students could not afford new shoes. Amal raised her hand in the council meeting. "This rule," she said, "feels unfortunate and unfair. Some students try their best but do not have the means."
"It's about order," said a teacher.
"But order should never come before compassion," Amal replied.
Another representative whispered, "That rule sounds… unconstitutional."
They voted. The rule was changed. Amal felt her heart flutter. Change could be slow — but it was real.
One evening, she and Nora sat on their beds, both doing homework.
"You've changed," Nora said. "You used to be so quiet."
"I had to adapt," Amal replied. "And you?"
Nora shrugged. "I'm learning too. Being right all the time doesn't mean being respected."
They shared a laugh. It was small — but it felt honest.
During essay week, Amal wrote a piece called "Growing From the Middle." She used words like productive, symbiotic, and fragile.
"A school is like a tree," she wrote. "It needs deep roots of respect, branches of growth, and leaves that fall and come again. Every person here, whether popular or unpopular, makes it grow. Sometimes a fragile moment becomes the start of strength."
Her teacher wrote at the bottom, "Your voice is becoming more noticeable."
At the end of the term, Amal called home. "I didn't win," she told her father.
"But you changed something," he said. "That's better than winning."
She smiled. "I think I remembered who I was after all."

comprehension.question: What is the difference between a need and a want? Give one example of each from the passage.
comprehension.correctAnswer: A need is something you must have to live safely and healthily, such as food, clean water, shelter or clothing, while a want is something nice to have but not essential, such as a new toy or extra sweets after school.
comprehension.explanation: The passage explains that a need is something you must have to live safely and healthily, such as food, clean water, shelter or clothing, while a want is nice to have but not essential, like a new toy or extra sweets after school.

comprehension.question: The passage says "Money is a tool." What does this mean?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It means that money is not good or bad by itself; what matters is how a person chooses to use it.
comprehension.explanation: The passage says money is not good or bad on its own; what matters is how we use it. So calling money a tool means the person using it decides whether it does good.

comprehension.question: According to the passage, what three parts could you divide your pocket money into?
comprehension.correctAnswer: You could divide it into one part for saving, one part for spending on things you need or enjoy, and one part for giving to charity or helping your family.
comprehension.explanation: Look at the paragraph about budgets: it says you could divide pocket money into one part for saving, one part for spending on things you need or enjoy, and one part for giving to charity or helping your family.

comprehension.question: What does the passage say about comparing prices at the market?

comprehension.explanation: In the paragraph about comparing prices, the passage says noticing which shop sells rice more cheaply or which soap lasts longer means you get better value, and it calls this a form of critical thinking.

comprehension.question: Why does the passage say a person with a meagre income can be more successful than someone with a large fortune?

comprehension.explanation: Near the end, the passage says what matters is being wise with whatever resources you have, so a person who manages a meagre income well can be far more successful than someone who wastes a large fortune.

grammar.title: Comparative Adverbs
grammar.explanation: Comparative adverbs let us compare how two actions are done, showing that one action happens in a greater or lesser way than another, such as more quickly or faster.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Comparative adverbs compare how two actions are done. The form depends on the length of the adverb.
Rule 1 — short adverbs (one syllable) add -er: fast → faster ("He runs faster than his sister."); hard → harder ("She works harder than anyone in the class."); late → later ("They arrived later than expected.").
Rule 2 — longer adverbs (two or more syllables) take "more" in front: quickly → more quickly ("She adapted more quickly than I did."); carefully → more carefully ("He counted the coins more carefully than before.").
Rule 3 — irregular forms are learned by heart: well → better, badly → worse, far → farther or further.
Always use "than" to show what is being compared: "He saves money more wisely than his older brother."
grammar.commonMistake: Adding -er to a long adverb, as in "quicklier", or dropping "than" from the comparison, as in "He works harder I do."
grammar.memoryTip: One syllable, add -er (fast → faster); two or more syllables, put "more" in front (quickly → more quickly). Treat "more" as the helper for longer words.
grammar.practice:
Part A — write the correct comparative form of the adverb in brackets: 1) My brother plays video games (badly) than I do. 2) She solved the problem (quickly) than I expected. 3) He speaks (softly) than his friend. 4) The bus arrived (late) than usual. 5) She sings (beautifully) than anyone in the choir.
Part B — choose the correct form: 6) She adapted to school life (more easily / easilier) than she expected. 7) He runs (faster / more fast) than anyone in his year. 8) She performed (better / more good) in the second test.

Answer key — Part A: 1. worse (badly is irregular: badly → worse) — "My brother plays video games worse than I do."; 2. more quickly — "She solved the problem more quickly than I expected."; 3. more softly — "He speaks more softly than his friend."; 4. later — "The bus arrived later than usual."; 5. more beautifully — "She sings more beautifully than anyone in the choir." Part B: 6. more easily (not "easilier"); 7. faster (not "more fast"); 8. better (not "more good").

grammar.title: Quantifiers
grammar.explanation: Quantifiers tell us how much or how many of something there is, such as both, neither, some, many, few and a lot of.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A quantifier goes before a noun to show amount. Use "both" for two things ("Both students saved their pocket money.") and "neither" for two things when you mean not one of them ("Neither answer was negative."). Use "some", "many", "few" and "a lot of" for larger groups: "Some children prefer to spend rather than save."; "Many families give to charity regularly."; "Only a few students forgot their homework."; "There are a lot of stalls at the market." Use "each" and "every" for individual members of a group: "Each student received pocket money."; "Every choice you make with money is practice."
"Both" takes a plural verb ("Both students were ready"); "neither" takes a singular verb ("Neither student was ready").
grammar.commonMistake: Using "both" with a singular noun ("Both student had ideas"), or pairing "neither" with another negative to make a double negative ("Neither of them did not come").
grammar.memoryTip: Think of "both" as a pair, like a pair of shoes, taking a plural verb, and "neither" as "not one of two", taking a singular verb.
grammar.practice:
Part A — choose the correct quantifier: 1) ______ of the answers were correct. (both / neither) 2) I saw ______ cats in the garden. (some / many) 3) ______ of the two friends could come to the party. (Both / Neither) 4) There are ______ apples in the basket. (few / a lot of) 5) ______ student must bring their own pencil. (Each / Many)
Part B — fill the blank: 6) ______ of the two brothers saved their pocket money. 7) She checked ______ item on her shopping list. 8) There were ______ people at the market this morning.

Answer key — Part A: 1. Both (agrees with the plural verb "were": "Both of the answers were correct." "Neither" would need the singular verb "was"); 2. either "some" or "many" is correct — "cats" is plural and the sentence gives no clue about the exact amount, so both quantifiers fit; "some" is the more everyday choice, "many" stresses a bigger number; 3. either "Both" or "Neither" is grammatically correct here, since "could" doesn't change form for singular or plural — pick whichever matches the story you have in mind: "Both of the two friends could come to the party" or "Neither of the two friends could come to the party"; 4. either "few" or "a lot of" is correct with the plural noun "apples" — choose "few" for a nearly empty basket or "a lot of" for a full one; 5. Each (agrees with the singular noun "student"; "many" would need the plural "students"). Part B: 6. either "Both" or "Neither" works, for the same reason as Part A #3 — the sentence doesn't say whether the brothers succeeded; 7. either "each" or "every" is correct before the singular noun "item"; 8. any quantifier for a larger group is correct here — "many", "a lot of" and "some" all fit before the plural noun "people".

grammar.title: Reflexive Pronouns
grammar.explanation: Reflexive pronouns — myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves and themselves — are used when the subject and object of a sentence are the same person.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A reflexive pronoun ends in -self (singular) or -selves (plural) and matches the subject: I → myself, you → yourself, he → himself, she → herself, it → itself, we → ourselves, they → themselves.
Use 1 — subject and object are the same: "She looked at herself in the mirror."; "They taught themselves to budget."
Use 2 — for emphasis, to stress that someone acted without help: "I baked the cake myself."; "The children organised the event themselves."
grammar.commonMistake: Writing "hisself" or "theirselves" instead of "himself" and "themselves", or using a reflexive pronoun when the subject and object are different people ("She told myself the news").
grammar.memoryTip: If the action bounces back to the person who did it, like a ball off a wall, reach for a "self" word.
grammar.practice:
Part A — fill in the correct reflexive pronoun: 1) She taught ______ how to make a budget. 2) We organised the charity sale by ______. 3) He accidentally hurt ______ while cutting the paper. 4) The cat washed ______ after playing in the mud. 5) I reminded ______ to save my pocket money. 6) They prepared ______ for the big exam.
Part B — add a reflexive pronoun for emphasis: 7) "I will do it ______," said Amal. 8) Did you all enjoy ______ at the school fair?

Answer key — Part A: 1. herself; 2. ourselves; 3. himself; 4. itself; 5. myself; 6. themselves. Part B: 7. myself; 8. yourselves.

grammar.title: Reported Speech (Introduction)
grammar.explanation: Reported (indirect) speech tells what someone said without quoting their exact words; we usually move the tense back one step and change the pronouns to match the new speaker.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
To report speech, change the pronouns, move the tense back one step, remove the quotation marks and add a reporting verb like "said" or "asked".
Direct: "I love mangoes." → Reported: She said she loved mangoes.
Direct: "We are going to the park." → Reported: They said they were going to the park.
Direct: "Can you help me?" → Reported: He asked if I could help him.
Direct: "Please finish your homework." → Reported: The teacher told us to finish our homework.
grammar.commonMistake: Forgetting to shift the tense ("She said she is tired") or keeping the quotation marks after the reporting verb ("She said, 'she was frustrated.'").
grammar.memoryTip: Report it like a story you are retelling: step the tense back one and swap the pronouns to fit the new speaker.
grammar.practice:
Change the direct speech into reported speech: 1) "I will help you." → She said ________. 2) "I am reading a book." → He said ________. 3) "Do you like mangoes?" → She asked ________. 4) "We are saving money for the school trip." → They said ________.

Answer key: 1. She said (that) she would help me. ("I" → "she"; "will" → "would"; "you", the person spoken to, → "me", following the same shift used in the rule's own example, "Can you help me?" → "He asked if I could help him."); 2. He said (that) he was reading a book. ("I" → "he"; "am reading" → "was reading"); 3. She asked if I liked mangoes. ("you" → "I"; "do you like" → "if I liked", the same question pattern as the rule's example); 4. They said (that) they were saving money for the school trip. ("we" → "they"; "are saving" → "were saving"). The exact pronoun for "you" can change if you imagine a different listener, but the tense shift (back one step) and the removal of quotation marks must stay the same in every answer.

grammar.title: Connecting Words
grammar.explanation: Connecting words such as firstly, however, therefore, in addition and finally link ideas smoothly and show how one point relates to the next.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Connecting words usually start a sentence or clause and are followed by a comma. Firstly introduces the first point ("Firstly, saving money teaches patience."); however shows a contrast ("I wanted to save; however, I spent it on snacks."); therefore shows a result ("She saved every week; therefore, she had enough for the school trip."); in addition adds a point ("In addition, budgeting helps families."); finally signals the last point; in conclusion sums up ("In conclusion, financial literacy is a crucial skill.").
grammar.commonMistake: Forgetting the comma after a connecting word at the start of a sentence, as in "However I don't eat it often."
grammar.memoryTip: Picture connecting words as bridges between two ideas; the comma is the small step you take just after you cross.
grammar.practice:
Fill each blank with the best connecting word (Firstly, However, Therefore, Finally, In addition): 1) I woke up late this morning. ______, I missed the bus. 2) ______, we will go over the rules of the game. 3) I studied for the test. ______, I felt confident. 4) We had a lot of fun at the party. ______, we danced all evening! 5) Saving money is important. ______, it teaches us to plan.

Answer key: 1. Therefore (missing the bus is a result of waking up late); 2. Firstly (introduces the first point before explaining the rules); 3. Therefore (feeling confident is a result of studying); 4. Finally (names the last, standout part of the fun evening); 5. In addition (adds a further reason why saving money matters). "However" is not needed for any of these five sentences because none of them show a contrast.

grammar.title: Tone Awareness
grammar.explanation: Tone is the mood your word choice creates; adverbs like eagerly, firmly and dramatically can make the same message feel excited, serious or over-the-top.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Choose adverbs that match the feeling you want your reader to have. In "The Notice Board", Amal learns that tone matters: when she spoke firmly, people listened (a serious, confident tone); when she spoke aggressively, they pushed back (a harsh tone); when she spoke dramatically, they laughed (an over-the-top tone). The same message can have very different effects depending on the tone.
grammar.commonMistake: Choosing a word whose tone clashes with the meaning, such as "The puppy firmly wagged its tail" when a playful word like "happily" fits better.
grammar.memoryTip: Tone is the music of your writing — pick your words the way you pick a song to match the mood you want.
grammar.practice:
Complete each sentence with dramatically, firmly or eagerly: 1) The chef ______ presented her new dish to the judges. 2) The teacher spoke ______ when explaining the importance of studying. 3) The puppy bounced ______ when it saw its owner. 4) The actor ______ dropped to one knee during the play. 5) The student spoke ______ during the debate, making her point clear.

Answer key: 1. dramatically — the chef presents her dish with theatrical flair; 2. firmly — a serious, confident tone fits explaining something important; 3. eagerly — an excited puppy greeting its owner; 4. dramatically — dropping to one knee during a play is a theatrical, over-the-top action; 5. firmly — making a point clearly in a debate calls for a serious, confident tone.

writing.title: Writing 1: Opinion Essay on Pocket Money
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write an opinion essay about pocket money and saving. State your opinion clearly in the introduction, give your strongest reason with an example (begin with "Firstly"), add a second reason (use "In addition" or "Furthermore"), and finish with a conclusion (use "In conclusion"). Include at least two comparative adverbs and two quantifiers.
writing.modelText:
I believe children should save some of their pocket money instead of spending it all.
Firstly, saving teaches patience. My friend Sami puts most of his money in a tin and waits three days before he buys anything, so he spends more carefully than he used to. In addition, saving turns a meagre amount into something substantial. A few shillings a week grew into enough for New Year gifts for his whole family.
In conclusion, pocket money is a privilege, and savers learn to use it more wisely than eager spenders at the tuck shop.

items: Introduction (opinion stated clearly): I believe children should save some of their pocket money instead of spending it all straight away.

Firstly, paragraph 2 (strongest reason with an example): Firstly, saving teaches patience. My cousin Idil keeps most of her money in a tin and waits several days before she buys anything, so she spends far more carefully than she used to.
In addition, paragraph 3 (second reason): In addition, saving turns a meagre amount into something substantial. A few coins each week grew steadily into enough for new school shoes by December.
Conclusion: In conclusion, pocket money is a privilege, and children who save learn to use it more sensibly than those who spend eagerly at the tuck shop.
otherAnswers: Alternative opinion: I believe children should be free to spend most of their pocket money as they choose, because a little enjoyment now teaches its own lessons. Firstly, spending helps children learn the real value of things more quickly than simply watching a number grow in a tin. In addition, a few treats keep motivation high, since saving every coin for months can feel discouraging. In conclusion, some spending alongside a little saving is more balanced than saving almost everything.

Alternative reasoning, still pro-saving but with different examples: I believe saving pocket money matters because emergencies happen without warning. Firstly, an unexpected school trip is far easier to afford when a family already has some savings set aside. In addition, most banks pay a small amount of interest, so saved money quietly grows on its own. In conclusion, a family with even a little saved money copes with surprises more calmly than one with none.

writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a six-sentence paragraph about the difference between needs and wants. Begin with a topic sentence, join ideas with and, but or because, and use at least two vocabulary words from this unit.
writing.modelText: Needs and wants are different, and knowing the difference is crucial for managing money. A need is something you cannot live without, such as food, water and a safe home. A want is something fabulous but not necessary, like sweets from the tuck shop or a new football. Sometimes a want feels unavoidable because everybody else has it. But if you buy every want, your savings stay meagre and you feel frustrated later. I try to pay for needs first, and then I decide calmly whether a want is worth it.

items: Sentence 1 (topic sentence, joined with and): Needs and wants are different, and understanding the difference is crucial for managing money wisely.
Sentence 2 (need example): A need is something you cannot live without, such as food, clean water and a safe home.
Sentence 3 (want example): A want is something fabulous but not necessary, like new trainers or an extra snack from the tuck shop.
Sentence 4 (joined with because): Sometimes a want feels unavoidable because everybody else seems to have it already.
Sentence 5 (joined with but): But if you buy every want, your savings stay meagre and you feel frustrated later on.
Sentence 6 (closing, personal habit): I try to pay for needs first, and then I decide calmly whether a want is really worth it.

writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a heading and five accurate facts about saving or budgeting money. Use precise unit vocabulary, order your facts sensibly, and check your spelling and punctuation.
writing.modelText:
Five Facts About Saving Money
1. A budget is a plan that divides money into needs, wants, savings and giving.
2. Needs, such as food and rent, must be paid before any wants.
3. Even a meagre amount, like a few shillings a week, becomes substantial after a year.
4. Waiting three days before buying something is a productive way to avoid wasting money.
5. Money kept in a bank is safer than money in a tin, because a tin can be lost or stolen and a bank account can earn interest.

Fact 3: Even a meagre amount saved each week becomes substantial after a full year.
Fact 4: Waiting a few days before buying something is a productive way to avoid spending on impulse.
Fact 5: Money kept in a bank is usually safer than money in a tin at home, because a tin can be lost or stolen.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Not thinking that you are better than others; modest. Even though he won the race, he remained humble and thanked his friends for their support.
In a way that shows you really want to do something. She eagerly opened her birthday presents.
Not enough; very small in amount or quality. The meal was meagre, with only a small piece of bread and a little bit of soup.
In a strong and steady way; not easily moved or changed. She held the rope firmly so it would not slip from her hands.
Easily affected by things around you, like feelings or physical things. She is very sensitive and can easily feel sad when her friends are upset.
Feeling uneasy or not relaxed. I felt uncomfortable sitting on the hard chair for a long time.
Something that is not certain or may not be true. The story he told was questionable because it did not seem real.
Feeling upset because you cannot do something you want to do. I felt frustrated when I could not solve the maths problem.
Friendly and welcoming to guests or visitors. My grandmother is very hospitable; she always makes sure everyone feels comfortable when they visit.
Someone who is very forceful or ready to fight. The dog was aggressive and barked loudly at strangers.
